To anyone listening closely to what Microsoft CEO
Satya Nadella
has been saying over the past couple of years, this week felt like the clearest sign yet that AI is about to fundamentally change the size of Microsoft’s workforce. Microsoft is now offering voluntary buyouts
to around 60,000 employees
across the US, UK, Canada, and India.
It’s the first time the company has presented such an offer to so many employees, expanding greatly upon the
retirement offer
that was limited to around 9,000 employees earlier this year. It’s all part of an ongoing effort to avoid reducing investment in AI infrastructure by lowering Microsoft’s operating costs and headcount.
“Our total people costs will go down, our cost per head will go up, and my GPU per researcher will go up,” Nadella said
on a podcast
almost two years ago, responding to a question about AI’s impact on headcount. That’s a financial way of saying Microsoft will have fewer people, but it will offer higher salaries and more tools and AI power to those who remain.
It also helps explain the continued layoffs we’ve seen at Microsoft over the past couple of years. Microsoft has been performing layoffs regularly over the past decade, but over the past couple of years, the layoffs and
executive departures
have been significant.
These aren’t the annual layoffs of old; they’re now happening every few months. This week’s voluntary exit offer arrived just months after Microsoft
laid off 4,800 employees
, cuts that impacted its Xbox and commercial sales teams the most.
For the first time in a decade, Microsoft’s overall headcount has also gone
down year over year
. Microsoft now employs around 223,000 people as of June 30th, 5,000 fewer than the 228,000 people it employed in 2025. Microsoft
laid off 4 percent
of its workforce in July last year, and it’s now offering voluntary buyout offers to around a quarter of its employees.
More than 30 percent of the 9,000 eligible employees accepted a retirement offer earlier this year, but that number will likely be far less for the company’s latest Voluntary Exit Offer. That’s largely because, according to sources familiar, the offer is practically the same as regular severance terms at Microsoft — cash based on time at the company, accelerated stock vesting, some additional subsidized health coverage, and several months of career services.
But what makes this unusual is the scale of the amount of employees who have been offered this exit. Even if only 5 percent accept the offer, that’s still 3,000 employees. I understand eligible employees have until December to decide, so we won’t know the impact of this offer for a while yet. With rumors of more layoffs in November and January, the amount of employees who do accept will surely inform Microsoft’s numbers for its next round of cuts.
There are some, both inside and outside the company, who think Microsoft needs these cuts. “Microsoft needs fewer people,”
says
Merill Fernando
, a former Microsoft Entra product manager. “I’ve been on the inside. I’ve seen how things get built. Lots of small orgs. Layers on layers. Silos everywhere.”
Fernando paints a picture of a Microsoft where every organization “had its own priorities and its own decision makers,” so it’s hard to get the company to do anything collectively. It sounds a little like the meme where each organization in Microsoft is pointing guns at each other, competing instead of collaborating.
Nadella even addressed that meme last year in
a podcast
with Stripe co-founder
John Collison
, acknowledging that the comic has defined Microsoft’s cultural narrative “more so than reality,” but that it had signaled some very real tensions inside the company. “In some sense, some of these divisional tensions are real issues that need to have tension. Social cohesion is not a goal, winning in the marketplace is a goal,” said Nadella.
The question now is whether Nadella can reshape Microsoft for the AI era without undoing the cultural transformation that helped define his leadership. A company that has shifted to be
built around empathy
is now asking its employees to reckon with an AI future that could make many of their jobs unnecessary. How Nadella handles that transition will define his legacy as much as the growth and success he’s achieved over the past decade.
Xbox’s architect of Forza Motorsport is leaving after nearly 27 years
A few weeks ago I started hearing from Xbox employees that
Dan Greenawalt
, the longtime creative force behind
Forza Motorsport
, is leaving after almost 27 years. Greenawalt is departing as the head of Turn 10 Studios, the
Forza Motorsport
creator that merged with
Forza Horizon
developer Playground Games.
Playground Games studio head
Trevor Williams
revealed the news in a recent internal memo, seen by
Notepad
. “Dan Greenawalt has decided that this is the right time for him to retire from Microsoft,” says Williams. Greenawalt will stay on as an adviser to Williams and the newly appointed Playground Games chief operating officer, Michel Bastien, “while he transitions to his next phase.” Here’s part of Williams’ memo about Greenawalt:
It’s hard to overstate Dan’s impact over the past 27 years. From shipping Project Gotham Racing on the original XBOX in 2001 to leading the creation of Forza, founding Turn 10 Studios and appearing so many times on our E3 stage, usually making a dramatic entrance with a supercar in tow – and so much more – we owe tremendous thanks and gratitude to Dan. On behalf of both teams, I would like to thank Dan for his leadership, his support, and his partnership. I wish him well for whatever comes next.
Microsoft revealed last month that it was
merging its two Forza developers
into a single studio as part of a
massive restructuring of Xbox
. Both Playground Games and Turn 10 Studios have merged into just Playground Games. The studio now has two locations: Playground Games Leamington Spa and Playground Games Redmond.
With Greenawalt retiring and Turn 10 merged into Playground Games, it’s not clear if we’ll ever see Microsoft return to
Forza Motorsport
. More than 70 people at Turn 10 Studios were
laid off last year
, in a move that hit the vast majority of the studio. Over the past year, Turn 10 Studios has essentially been maintaining
Forza Motorsport
, and now the remaining employees have moved to Playground Games to work on
Forza Horizon
and
Fable
.
It’s time to name The Elders Scrolls VI: Sentinel
It’s been more than eight years since Bethesda
officially announced
the existence of the sixth game in its
Elder Scrolls
series. While there have been some debates around
platform exclusivity
for
The Elder Scrolls VI
, we’ve heard very little detail about the game that Bethesda has been working on all this time.
Sources familiar with Bethesda’s plans tell me that the Xbox-owned publisher is about to announce that the next
Elder Scrolls
game will officially be called
The Elder Scrolls VI: Sentinel
. The announcement could come as soon as next month, during a period that will mark 15 years since
The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim
was released.
Bethesda has been showing off
Sentinel
gameplay in recent months, I’m told. Xbox CEO
Asha Sharma
got a live playthrough of
Sentinel
in August, and
she praised
the scale of the game and said “the story is even greater.”
While I’m only expecting a name reveal next month and nothing more, I’ve been hearing some additional details about the game. If you want to totally avoid spoilers about the game, then don’t read the next paragraph.
I understand that
Sentinel
will be set in Hammerfell, a province in the Elder Scrolls universe that’s appeared in
The Elder Scrolls Adventures: Redguard
and
The Elder Scrolls Online
.
Sentinel
will be the first game about the history of the Elder Scrolls, and help uncover the secrets of these mysterious ancient artifacts.
The pad
Xbox’s first chief operating officer is out after just a few months.
This is a weird one.
Helen Chiang
is
leaving Microsoft after 21 years
. She previously served as the head of
Minecraft
before being promoted to Xbox COO in July. The sudden departure was announced in a surprisingly short memo from Xbox chief Asha Sharma last week. “Helen Chiang is leaving Microsoft today. I’m grateful for her years of service and wish her well,” says Sharma. It doesn’t seem like the Xbox COO position is going away, as Sharma notes that “we’ll share more on COO leadership as plans are finalized.”
Eurogamer
reported
over the weekend that Chiang had been “terminated for policy violations.” I’ve heard similar chatter internally, but Chiang has been described to me by multiple Xbox employees as highly respected, with high integrity, so this turn of events is quite odd. I’m trying to get more details, but if you’ve heard anything, please reach out confidentially at
notepad@theverge.com
or through the secure Signal messaging app. (
I’m tomwarren.01
.)
Microsoft’s new Surface Laptop Ultra update fixes reboot and display bugs.
I ran into some weird issues with the Surface Laptop Ultra during my review, and Microsoft is now fixing some of them
with a firmware update
. The update addresses screen flickering, unexpected restarts, and lengthy reboot times alongside unspecified “additional bug fixes and general performance improvements.” I’m still waiting to see if Nvidia or Microsoft addresses the strange laggy feeling on the Surface Laptop Ultra, and it’s too early to say whether this firmware update addresses that or not yet.
GitHub’s former CEO launched a competing platform for AI agents.
We knew that Thomas Dohmke, former GitHub CEO, was building some kind of competitor to GitHub, but the result has surprised people internally during the week of GitHub’s Universe conference. Developers can use the
new Entire platform
to host and review code, but it’s also designed to work with AI agents and replaces pull requests with a “Trails” feature that offers “customizable evals that are scored by agents on every code push.” One GitHub employee tells me, “people are shocked, they have ambushed us up and down the stack on our own conference week.”
Windows will soon let you perform an internet speed test without opening your browser.
Microsoft added a speed test option to the Windows 11 taskbar earlier this year, but it was just a link to a speed test in Bing that opened in your browser. Now, Microsoft is actually
integrating a full speed test into the taskbar
, so you can right-click the network icon and perform an internet speed test right there.
Windows 11 is getting some neat trackpad features.
Microsoft is adding
new Windows trackpad features
that let you scroll through long documents and webpages faster. You’ll also be able to continuously scroll through a page by swiping the edge of your touchpad, along with support for single-finger scrolling. It’s the small things that count, and I love to see these kinds of features being added to Windows.
Microsoft says its AI tool is better than doctors at diagnosing conditions.
Microsoft claims to have developed an AI-powered tool that it says can
diagnose conditions up to four times more accurately than human doctors
. The findings were published last week in
Science

Some users aren’t exactly thrilled with The New York Times’ recipe-tweaking AI tool.
Some users aren’t exactly thrilled with The New York Times’ recipe-tweaking AI tool.
by
Jess Weatherbed
Oct 29, 2026, 2:39 PM UTC

Gift
The AI tool provides recommendations and adjusts the recipe accordingly.
Image: The New York Times
Jess Weatherbed
is a news writer focused on creative industries, computing, and internet culture. Jess started her career at TechRadar, covering news and hardware reviews.
The New York Times
is testing a new AI feature for its Cooking app that helps users to modify recipes, and it has sparked some drama among users. Last Friday,
NYT
Cooking senior editor Genevieve Ko
announced the feature
, which can be used to
recommend substitutions
for ingredients and cooking equipment, scale recipes to any number of servings, and “generally make our recipes work for what a cook needs at that moment.”
One of the examples given in the article shows a user asking to use baby spinach instead of kale, with the Cooking app feature advising that because baby spinach wilts faster, it should be added during a later step of the recipe. Ko says it can also change the recipes around different pans and tools. Customized recipes are private and can’t be published or shared through the app. The AI modification feature is being rolled out gradually while the
NYT
monitors how it performs — it’s currently available to all Cooking subscribers on the iOS app, and it will be more broadly available “soon.”
Some
NYT
readers have pushed back against the feature, citing concerns in the article’s comment section around the environmental impact of widespread AI adoption and the general impact that AI features may have on the user experience. When one user asked if there will be a way to disable the AI feature, Ko responded with, “No, not at this time,” and noted that the feature is “completely optional to use.”
The tool adds a chatbot text box interface on the lower screen of recipes, and it requires you to agree to some terms and conditions before you use it.
Image: Jennifer Pattison Tuohy /
The Verge
“Unbelievably disappointing to see,” said another
NYT
user. “I’ve always loved NYT Cooking and it pains me that the AI mandate has reached what used to be a wonderful and simple collection of recipes and notes from all sorts of different people.”
This isn’t the first time that AI has been used by the NYT Cooking app. Ko says it was used to convert imperial volume measurements to metric weight measurements in recipes two years ago, and a feature was added last year that converts recipes to halve or double the original serving size. The comments on the new AI feature announcement post have since been closed, but
NYT
spokesperson Jordan Cohen tells
The Verge
that this is
standard practice
:
“Comments on this article remained open for four days, with editors from Cooking taking care to answer questions, address concerns and engage directly with readers. We kept that conversation open to give readers a meaningful opportunity to share feedback and hear from the team. Closing comments on older articles is standard practice at The Times so that our moderators can focus on new discussions. We’re pleased to see that many members of our Cooking community are interested in exploring this tool and are already trying it out on our iOS app; they’re reporting good results.”

articles.content:
Podcasts
AI
Business
Anthropic is asking Wall Street to believe in AGI
SemiAnalysis’ Joey Brookhart helps break down the Anthropic S-1 and why he thinks the company could be worth $10 trillion.
by
Nilay Patel
Oct 29, 2026, 2:00 PM UTC
Link
Share
Nilay Patel
is editor-in-chief of The Verge, host of the
Decoder podcast
, and co-host of
The Vergecast
.
Today on
Decoder
, I’m joined by Joey Brookhart, an analyst at the chip and AI research firm SemiAnalysis, to help me dig into the story inside the numbers of the Anthropic IPO filing — a document known as an S-1.
Anthropic just
filed its S-1 to go public
on the Nasdaq, and it could start trading as soon as next month at a valuation of anywhere between $1.5 trillion and $2 trillion. That would immediately make it one of the most valuable companies on the planet.
But the price tag really isn’t the whole story here. The S-1 document published earlier this week is hundreds upon hundreds of pages
filled with details
that finally paint a picture of the economics of a frontier AI lab. As you might imagine, that picture is both really complicated and built on a series of very, very
ambitious assumptions about the future and what AI will do to it
.
So I wanted to have Joey on the show to help break down what this document tells us, both about Anthropic’s finances and the broader AI economy. Joey and his colleagues at SemiAnalysis actually
built a model of Anthropic’s finances from the outside
back in July, so he’s been waiting for this filing about as eagerly as anyone, and I was excited to hear his take on what we’ve learned and, importantly, what we still don’t know.
Okay: SemiAnalysis’ Joey Brookhart on the Anthropic S-1 and the costs and risks of building frontier AI. Here we go.
This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.
Joey Brookhart, you are an analyst at SemiAnalysis. You’re also co-lead on SemiAnalysis’ Tokenomics model, which is going to come up a lot in this episode. Welcome to
Decoder
.
Yeah, thanks so much, Nilay.
I am very excited to talk to you. We’re talking just a couple days after the big Anthropic S-1 was filed. It’s our first look inside of the finances of one of the leading frontier models. What’s your take? What’s your read into it?
It was an awesome S-1. It’s been a rough three weeks since the investor day. Some people were somewhat disappointed in the September [annualized recurring revenue] numbers, but what we saw here was a company that has efficiently scaled to an amazing level, with a $1 trillion-plus valuation, $70 billion-plus of ARR in a very short amount of time.
In gross margins, compute margins, and free cash flow, everything is what you’d want to see. So I don’t think there was much to nitpick in this filing. It’s the reason you’ve seen a lot of the semiconductor complex, and the neoclouds and compute stocks, really rally again in the last two days.
It’s funny, I don’t think I can nitpick the S-1 itself. I want to get into some of the details because there are a lot of numbers in there that are worth thinking about. I actually just want to start at the really big picture. You run a thing called Tokenomics. I’m going to explain what Tokenomics is to people.
I look at Anthropic and where it could go. I look at Dario Amodei saying that he can see his way to $1 trillion in revenue. Where does that money come from? Because so much of these businesses are about eating every other business and it feels like someone else has to make some money to pay Anthropic to generate these revenues. I haven’t actually seen that laid out very clearly.
Verge
subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free
Decoder
wherever you get your podcasts. Head
here
. Not a subscriber? You can
sign up here
.
It’s so interesting. Today, because even the scale we’re at is $120 billion of ARR between the two leading labs, it’s still an extremely narrow market. The top 1 percent of customers are the ones that are spending $50,000 to $100,000 per employee. Your broader Fortune 500 or Global 2000, which typically do a lot of IT spend, isn’t spending much.
A lot of the spending, especially at Anthropic, is coding-specific. It’s almost a single vertical company. We look in the future to 2027, you think to this broader adoption and white collar work. This typical enterprise Q4 budgeting season, we actually haven’t gone through with one of these labs yet in any meaningful way because their ARR did really start to accelerate until the beginning of the year. We think of other cases like cyber, which can be similar to coding, where these are eight-figure-plus contracts with leading enterprises that can scale very quickly due to all the cybersecurity incidents we’re seeing. You get to other verticals like bio.
To get to $1 trillion, we do have to move to some of that white collar work, where it goes from AI augmentation to labor saving or replacement in some areas. You look at things like
Microsoft’s buyout offers to employees as an example of this
, but there’s no wealth of other verticals that they can get into and really start to move the needle.
This is the single biggest question I have, not just about the S-1, but the entire industry. I would understand that if there are one or two leading labs. There are two big companies that have a technology that can automate a whole bunch of things. We will see how well that automation goes sector by sector, but there are not just two leading labs. There are quite a few of them. There are open weight models.
I’ve heard from a lot of CEOs who are very nervous about giving all their data to an OpenAI or Anthropic and they would like to run some things on-prem. There are law firms running on-prem AI now, which is the funniest turn in maybe all of history.
How do you see that playing out? Because so much of the pressure on this S-1 was the numbers themselves, which I want to talk about, but then there’s the external pressure of, “You’ve got to grow and growth is not as short.” So how do you see all of that playing out?
It’s very interesting because when we look at coding today, for example — and I think we saw this in Q3 with OpenAI kind of catching up — there are areas of coding where there are very low switching costs, and I can just move between that. What we hear from enterprises and maybe, too, on the OpenAI side — obviously I think they somewhat botched the Fable release, and the lack of zero data retention is why we saw some of the slowdown. That’s something they can fix with Fable 5.5 and maybe drive more enterprise adoption there.
That’s a huge thing for enterprises when we talk with them. We definitely see enterprises now, and more so, too, a lot of the AI natives, doing custom training and post-training on open weight models, and then running either their inference off of that or even their products for internal or external use cases.
Obviously, DeepMind at Google and [Meta Superintelligence Labs] are very well-funded labs that have pretty similar training compute capacity, and they’re bringing on a ton of it. Not even to mention SpaceX as well, with what Elon said on [about] 10 net new gigawatts next year and half of that is the long-term internal use case.
In the first half of the year, Anthropic ran away with it. They were 90 percent of the industry’s net new ARR. We saw in Q3 that OpenAI was probably actually the majority of industry net new ARR. Open-source has grown from probably $1 billion of token inference costs, ARR, in Q1 to $10 billion-plus here in Q3.
So yes, the industry’s gotten much more competitive, but there are all these new use cases, too, and some of these verticalized use cases are really where we’re going to see the growth going forward. Because it’s obvious coding isn’t going to power us to even triple from here.
It’s interesting. The concept is called Tokenomics. You run that practice alongside another co-lead at SemiAnalysis. Explain what it is because to me it’s such a smart way of thinking about, “We’re going to put some money in and maybe we’ll get some money out.”
I think of it as the unit economics [of AI], or even just the broader idea — everything from a macro- to microeconomics of running an AI business or even looking at AI demand. So we cover the hyperscalers, now some of the neoclouds as well in a separate product.
But then just the AI labs, too. For investors, or just people that are interested in the business, Anthropic had negative 94 percent gross margins on inference two years ago. Now they have a positive 85 percent margin, and people don’t understand how they allocate compute. How do we think about the inference business model?
Part of that gross margin conversation is the revenue per megawatt in inference. Why are all companies that are running inference seeing massive gains in inference and compute efficiency? So we try to model out these businesses and obviously when Anthropic was private, we’re dealing with information we can get from the press and things like that.
But now that we have concrete audited numbers, it’s easy to explain the unit economics of this. And also how the businesses differ. OpenAI is a much different business than Anthropic just in both their consumption versus subscription and then historical weight versus consumer versus enterprise. [We are] trying to understand across the demand level the economics of these businesses.
Several years ago when I talked to Google CEO Sundar Pichai about the cost of inference, I said, “How are you ever going to make money?” He was just very clear. He said, “If there’s one thing Google’s good at, it’s bringing this stuff down the cost curve.”
It was a very blunt answer. I understand how Google can do it. They make their own chips. Anthropic is running on everyone else’s clouds. The core part of the S-1 is how much they’ve committed to spend on other people’s clouds: SpaceXAI, Google, Amazon. Where does their efficiency come from?
There’s really token throughput. They have a very diverse chip fleet. Between Trainiums, TPUs, and GPUs, across all of those, we see a ton of token efficiencies. Token throughput, for example, on Trainium chips is up 5x to 10x year-over-year right now.
Dealing with both the hardware level efficiencies and the software — and how the model interacts with the hardware — there are a lot of token throughput gains where if you’re doing X tokens per second, now you’re doing five or 10 times that just a year later. What they’ll tell you is they see continued compute efficiencies as well going forward.
Max Kan, who co-leads Tokenomics model with me at SemiAnalysis, and I have even published some research on this. Right now, if Anthropic’s at $65 million of revenue per inference megawatt, this was mid-teens last year at this time. What we’ve said on maybe Opus 5.5 on a [Nvidia] Blackwell, you can get to $100 to $120 million of revenue per megawatt.
The big thing here is they’re paying on average now just a little over $10 million per megawatt in [cost of goods sold], or just in compute costs. What you can do with those margins is then reinvest in training.
People don’t realize this, but only about 30 percent of the compute is actually in inference-serving revenue. The rest is for experimentation and research, training models, and post-training models. So there’s a lot of compute that is building the next model and that’s more of the R&D side and where you actually get your returns and defensibility in this business.
Actually, what I was expecting to see in the S-1 was that dynamic play out much more strongly — that Anthropic makes a bunch of money selling the models they have now and there are more customers in the future for the models they have now. That’s going to throw off a whole bunch of margin. And then, because it is Anthropic and they think they’re building a digital god, they’re going to train the next models as much as they can.
That is a very particular Anthropic story. The company is chasing AGI. The people who work there will hap

Anthropic’s business plan: Build God or die trying
Anthropic faces intense competitive pressure and huge fixed costs. Can Claude build itself fast enough to succeed?
by

Oct 29, 2026, 1:30 PM UTC
Link

Anthropic’s business plan: Build God or die trying
Anthropic faces intense competitive pressure and huge fixed costs. Can Claude build itself fast enough to succeed?
by
Elizabeth Lopatto
Oct 29, 2026, 1:30 PM UTC
Link
Share
Gift
Elizabeth Lopatto
is a reporter who writes about tech, money, and human behavior. She joined The Verge in 2014 as science editor. Previously, she was a reporter at Bloomberg.
The Anthropic S-1
seems to have provided the financial justification for the company to spend as much as it possibly can on compute. If you are the kind of person who wonders if Anthropic is doing its level best to build a machine god while convincing Wall Street it’s in the business of selling IT contracts, Anthropic has just offered a handy solution: Doing a bunch of things that look like you’re trying to build the machine god is the only way to avoid going bankrupt.
Forget about the machine god for a minute. At least in my read of the S-1, it seems like Anthropic is pinning the future of its company to dramatic growth; it has to, in order to meet its fixed costs. You don’t have to be an AI skeptic to lift an eyebrow at these numbers. But if you are skeptical that dramatic recursive self-improvement is possible — in the way the business plan seems to require — this doesn’t look like a good investment.
Let’s start with the good news for Anthropic fans. The company’s revenue grew
fourteen times
to $16.3 billion between the first half of 2026 and the first half of 2025. There’s an $80 billion loss, but it’s largely
an accounting thing that isn’t relevant to the underlying business
. If we remove that, and some other charges, including employee compensation, we’re looking at $1.62 billion in adjusted income in the first half of 2026. I’ve asked before if AI can
make enough money to pay for itself
, and the answer from Anthropic’s S-1 appears to be, at least for this company, at least right now, yes.
Anthropic names only OpenAI and Google as rivals
Anthropic was considerably more disciplined than OpenAI or Elon Musk, and it seems to be paying off. (Anthropic names only OpenAI and Google as rivals. Better luck next time, Elon!) The company has never released an AI image generator, an AI TikTok clone, or an AI waifu. Instead, it specialized in tasks like coding and cybersecurity, staying laser-focused on the thing it is easiest for a computer to do: more computer. And it focused on the enterprise market, which is less fickle than consumers. Its net revenue retention is 900 percent. Pretty good! That revenue isn’t consumers, either. About three-quarters of customers in the first half of 2026 are spending at least $100,000 a year.
On the other hand, Anthropic is under intense competitive pressure — from both other frontier labs
and
open-source models. The other frontier labs are all rushing for the cutting edge, too. Claude Opus 5.5 currently
sits atop the Epoch Capabilities Index
, but that leaderboard changes frequently. And for anyone who doesn’t care that their software is
four months behind
, there are the open-source ones.
What’s more, Anthropic has a disadvantage against a rival like Google. It doesn’t have multiple paths to revenue — and Google does. Google can also wrap its AI into other products businesses already use. Remember when
Microsoft Teams ate Slack
? It wasn’t because Teams was the better product; Microsoft just had better distribution, since Teams was bundled with other programs companies were already paying for. Having the best model matters more for cybersecurity — one area Anthropic is targeting for growth — than for instant messaging software, but it’s hard to compete on distribution.
There are some long-term commitments that highlight how intense the expansion pressure is on Anthropic
And also, revenue comes in spurts, usually after a new model is released. Between the competition and growth in use after each novel model, Anthropic can never stop training, and it has to do so more efficiently than its much larger competition.
So one important question is: Can Anthropic continue to provide the results we see in the S-1?
There are some long-term commitments that highlight how intense the expansion pressure is on Anthropic. Sure, there’s a convenient blank on its purchase commitments and lease agreements on page 64, and another kicky little blank on the amounts it’s expecting to spend before December 31st, 2030, on page 137. However, we know the commitments run through 2045.
Fortunately, there’s a “Commitments and contingencies” section that can help us out a little. There’s a fixed minimum of non-cancelable purchase commitments that total $265.6 billion, with terms between one and 20 years. The company has lease agreements “primarily related to compute and infrastructure capacity” that haven’t yet commenced of $321.4 billion, as of the unaudited June 30th figures. After that, Anthropic entered new compute and infrastructure agreements totaling about $245 billion, again with terms between one and 20 years. There’s some other transactions that haven’t yet been finalized, which Anthropic estimates as costing $125 billion to $150 billion. There are also other compute commitments that are variable.
“The S-1 does freeze in time a happy period when their initial models skyrocketed in usage.”
If I add all that up, I’m looking at a minimum of around $850 billion of commitments over the next 20 years, which will rise to about a trillion dollars if the transactions that haven’t been finalized are added in at the current estimated cost. And that’s assuming I’m not missing anything, which I may very well be.
So to meet those commitments, Anthropic’s growth must continue at breakneck speed. Anthropic doesn’t give us a payment schedule for its future commitments, but
analyst Harrison Rolfes of PitchBook
models it at about $90 billion a year from 2027 to 2030, which means $188 billion in revenue to keep the current ratio of cost to compute stable. “Growth is not optional for this company,” he writes. “The contracts assume it.”
Compute and infrastructure (and a few other items) associated with customers cost $2.3 billion in the first half of this year. Model development (and a few other items) was significantly more expensive; Anthropic spent $9.7 billion on it. But Anthropic simultaneously got more efficient — spending less money on compute to bring in each dollar of revenue, according to Rolfes.
Everyone in cybersecurity has to keep running just to stay in the same place, exactly like Anthropic
Is that a long-standing trend? Hard to say. We don’t have the third quarter numbers in front of us. “The S-1 does freeze in time a happy period when their initial models skyrocketed in usage and they didn’t have enough compute so they are able to charge more for what they had,” says Brendan Burke, an analyst at Futurum Group.
As enterprise software, it makes sense for Anthropic to target companies’ IT budgets. Conveniently, cybersecurity is a place where you will absolutely get your shit rekt if you are not constantly up to date — everyone there has to keep running just to stay in the same place,
exactly like Anthropic
. Of course, AI is part of the problem; hackers can use it to brute-force stuff they couldn’t do before. Plus, the products themselves are also causing headaches thanks to a partner’s sloppy fuck-up of
security protocols
around AI agents.
Frontier labs need high-margin products to avoid a race to the bottom on token pricing, notes Burke. That made something else stand out to me: Opus 5.5 reduced customer costs by 40 percent over Opus 5. Now, Anthropic says that lower cost means more usage, which lets the company preserve its margins. If you assume that cost reduction happens every time a new model is released, pretty soon you wind up with tasks at a fraction of the price.
Claude is already building Claude under human direction
This isn’t necessarily an insurmountable problem, in part because increased efficiency doesn’t always slash margins, says Gil Luria, an analyst with DA Davidson. Amazon Web Services and other cloud providers ”have become far more efficient every year and reduce their prices every year and they have had steady growth and rising margins,” he says.
But the pressure for growth is pretty undeniable. That’s where recursive self-improvement, with minimal or no supervision, comes in. “More capable models help our researchers discover these improvements faster; in turn, more powerful compute multipliers enable us to train even more capable models and deploy them more efficiently.” Based on the general rhetoric Anthropic has about the apocalypse or whatever, it expects to hit dramatic recursive self-improvement, maybe soon.
Claude is already building Claude under human direction. In its risk factors, Anthropic warns that it’s locked in to that approach. That comes with a clear tradeoff, since using AI to develop more AI “may cause the capabilities of our models to advance more rapidly than our ability to develop, validate, and implement corresponding safety, alignment, and security measures.” If I am reading that right, Anthropic is saying that its business relies on building new models so fast, using work it may not fully understand, that it is essentially forced, for business reasons, to do stuff that may be risky to everyone. Which is why we’ve got a bunch of weird stuff about the
existential
hazards of “catastrophic” harm
and the development of “forms of sentience” in the risk factors.
Is dramatic recursive self-improvement that escapes the bounds of human supervision possible? Dunno. But if it isn’t, that makes it much harder for Anthropic to meet its existing compute commitments and turn a
profit.

articles.content:
Oct 29, 2026, 10:00 AM GMT
A
A
hulking gray giant rises from the desert. Inside, engineers create the force behind our phones and computers and appliances, our streaming services and search engines and chatbots and vibe-coded apps and websites. The complex is simultaneously massive and squat, dwarfed by the mountains that surround it, and it is endless. I drive past one building, and then another, and then the ground opens up where construction crews have dug up the earth so a third building can rise. There is a parking lot, and then another, and then another. There is an empty lot on the other side of the street, full of cars and the occasional food truck to feed the thousands of laborers who are busy transforming this expanse of desert into an industrial park. There is dust, so much of it, choking the air.
I stand before the savior of Arizonaâs economy. Like all great deities, it demands sacrifice. In the desert, nothing is more precious than water, and water is what must be given â nearly 5 million gallons a day, every day, sourced from Phoenixâs municipal supply. The offering has been well worth it.
All of this is the fruit of the Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company, the worldâs leading producer of microchips. Its Arizona operation is the result of a pre-pandemic gamble Phoenix made to
revive its sluggish economy
, which never quite rebounded from the Great Recession. Now TSMCâs foundry looms over the cityâs outskirts.
TSMC is a success story, one that some local leaders may have hoped to repeat with hyperscale data center developments. The progression may have seemed natural: The Grand Canyon State is not only home to the largest chip factory this side of the Pacific but also
172 data centers
, neither of which faced much pushback. But the newer, larger developments being proposed from Phoenix to Tucson demand more of everything â more water, more power, more land â than Arizonans are willing to give. Where TSMC was welcomed with open arms and the first wave of data centers was largely ignored, new developments are facing mass backlash in Arizona, where a grassroots, surprisingly bipartisan coalition of residents has united against data centers.
Now the state has a sixth C, Arizona native Christine Mackay tells me. âChips.â
In reporting this story, I spoke to local activists and economic developers, elected officials and their angry constituents. I sat in on city council meetings where people lined up by the dozens to speak up against data center projects, and in cozy suburban homes where tight-knit groups of former strangers told me about the struggle that brought them together. I pored over maps of Arizonaâs dry, cracked landscape with laypeople who, over the past two years, have made themselves experts on zoning and land use and water consumption so they can understand the beast theyâre trying to fight. The locals on both sides of this debate claim to want the same thing: a better, more prosperous Arizona. Their visions for achieving it, however, are completely at odds.
In Arizona and elsewhere, data center developers have tried to win over locals by making enticing promises about the jobs, tax revenue, and infrastructure theyâll bring with them. All they ask for in exchange is water â and, they swear, not nearly as much of it as youâd expect. Some hyperscale data centers, like Googleâs facility in The Dalles, Oregon, use about 1.5 million gallons a day, about one-third of what TSMCâs Arizona complex consumes in the same timeframe. Those reassurances, however, arenât enough to assuage Arizonans, who now have to contend with the fact that the state
will soon lose access
to nearly 30 percent of the water it receives from the Colorado River.
Even now, as people across the country sour on AI and fight against data centers in their communities, TSMCâs Arizona operation hums along without significant opposition. And yet itâs impossible to make sense of why Arizonans are so opposed to new data center development without first understanding why they eagerly welcomed TSMC, even though both industries must contend with the issue that has plagued Arizona since its founding: There isnât enough water.
An irrigation canal that is part of the Central Arizona Project, which brings water to Phoenix from the Colorado River.
For as long as anyone could remember, business in Arizona revolved around the storied âfive Câsâ: cattle, copper, cotton, citrus, and climate, a catchall for the regionâs mild, salubrious winters, which locals say often more than make up for the sweltering summers.
Now the state has a sixth C, Arizona native Christine Mackay tells me. âChips.â
The TSMC development is, in a sense, Mackayâs doing. As the head of Phoenixâs economic development office, she spearheaded the effort that brought the Taiwanese giant to the Sonoran Desert. In 2020, while the global economy was all but shut down, TSMC made an announcement. The same forces that brought the world to a standstill had created even more demand for TSMCâs products, and in response, TSMC would be opening an advanced semiconductor foundry â a âfab,â in industry jargon â in Phoenix. Initially, TSMC predicted that it would pour $12 billion into Arizonaâs economy by 2029. Since then, TSMCâs projected expenditure in the state has ballooned to $265 billion, what the company touts as the largest foreign direct investment in US history.
The TSMC Arizona headquarters in Phoenix.
TSMC just put the finishing touches on its second fab in a formerly desolate swath of north Phoenix, with a third under construction and plans for several more underway. This buildout has been more than a decade in the making. TSMC started shopping around for a US location in 2016. That year, Mackay said, the company put out a request for proposals through a codename. No one won.
âWe arenât a group that takes no for an answer,â Mackay said proudly. Her office asked TSMC executives what they thought Arizona was missing, and then spent the next three years addressing their concerns. In 2019, Phoenix sent a delegation to Taiwan to share a new development plan for a science and technology park, the nucleus of which would be a factory, ideally one of TSMCâs fabs. âThey agreed they needed to come back and take another look at Phoenix,â Mackay told me. Her team showed them two locations: Laveen, Arizona, a suburb southwest of Phoenix, and, just north of the city, an undeveloped area roughly the size of Manhattan called Biscuit Flats, so named, Mackay told me, because âitâs as round and flat as a biscuit.â
âThat very day,â she recalled, âthey said, âThis could work.ââ
What followed was a flurry of development unlike anything the state has ever seen. TSMC has brought more than 3,500 jobs to the state, and an entire economy has sprung up to support the companyâs Arizona operation. Much like in Taiwan â where the company accounts for nearly one-tenth of Taiwanâs gross domestic product â TSMC has become, if not the center of the universe, then at least a galaxy unto itself. The company controls
an estimated 70 percent
of the global chip market, and its contracts with Apple and Nvidia alone make up more than one-third of its annual revenue. (Apple and Nvidia design their own chips, but they donât produce them. The complex manufacturing process is instead largely outsourced to TSMC.)
This semiconductor manufacturing facility has more than 3,500 employees.
TSMC has changed swaths of Phoenix â its landscape, its industries â and it has brought with it jobs and prosperity. Locals fear that the new hyperscale data center developments will do the former but not the latter, consuming resources while contributing little to the community. Mackay, who has worked as an economic developer for over 30 years, didnât experience significant pushback when she helped court data center developments in the past. âThe first 10 data centers I did look like pretty little office buildings,â she said.
The new developments being proposed are neither pretty nor little. Where earlier data centers were inconspicuous, the hyperscale facilities developers want to build in Arizona â often on rural farm or desert land â are both massive and incongruous. Despite the stateâs recently acquired reputation for sprawl, there are still plenty of places where, in the quiet desert stillness, you can sometimes hear a pack of coyotes howl in the middle of the night. There are dark-sky corridors and wild animals, ghost towns and saguaro forests. All of this, some locals say, could be sacrificed for the benefit of an industry that also poses an existential threat to humanity. There are ethical questions and environmental ones, debates over zoning and taxes and, most of all, over water. Yet the cities and the outlying suburbs keep growing, spreading in all directions until theyâre constrained by geography or bureaucracy or Indigenous sovereignty. And industry, somehow, keeps arriving, thirstier than ever.
In Mesa, Arizona, the EdgeCore PH03 data center â the largest data center in the state â stands right beside a residential neighborhood.
Year-round but especially in the summers, Arizonans tailor their routines to the elements. Drivers are careful not to get stuck in dust storms or monsoons. Joggers avoid going out in late mornings and early afternoons, when the heat is at its most intense. And on August 1st, at the peak of monsoon season, the No Desert Data Center Coalitionâs protest began in the early evening, when the sunâs punishing rays were starting to give way to a muted desert sunset.
About a dozen people showed up to the rally on the outskirts of Tucson, in front of the 290-acre site where Beale Infrastructure is building a 600-megawatt data center. Every few minutes, Vivek Bharathan, one of the organizers, reminded the protesters to stay hydrated. Children sprayed each other with water guns and dutifully accepted drinks from their parents. Mayra Duron, one of the attendees, brought a cooler of agua de jamaica to share with the group. The magenta beverage, she said, was full of electrolytes. Water â the lack of it, the need for it, the amount required to build a massive data center in the middle of the desert â was top of mind. A hand-painted banner expressed the overarching sentiment: BEALEâS DATA CENTER WILL SUCK US DRY.
âIf you feel the heat, please head home,â Bharathan told the small crowd. âIt is a hot day, and if they succeed in building a data center here, itâll be even hotter. We know these things
create heat islands
that can affect the surrounding area by over 10 degrees Fahrenheit.â Duron, a local macrame artist who incorporates cactus spines into her weaving, said she worried about how rising temperatures would affect the regionâs saguaros. âIn Phoenix, itâs hyper-industrialized,â she said, âand theyâve seen saguaros die left and right.â
Cars honked in support. Some drivers pumped their fists out their windows as they sped by. Arizonans werenât riled up about AI in 2019, when the TSMC project was announced, nor did they notice or care much about the previous data centers that were quietly built throughout the state. Things have changed. Tucson, it appears, is united in its opposition to the data center complex dubbed Project Blue. But the buildings are going up anyway.
Members of the No Desert Data Center Coalition pose for a portrait near the site of the Project Blue data center. From left:
Glenda Avalos
, Margo, Reed Spurling, Vivek Bharathan, and Pablo
.
âWe take it as normal because itâs been that way for so long. But it isnât normal. Itâs a catastrophe.â
Information about Project Blue began slowly trickling out in the spring of 2025. First came the name, and
some clues
: The development, whatever it was, would be on a county-owned plot of land; it would create 3,000 temporary construction jobs

Opinion: We urgently need to monitor AI agents’ actions in real time
—Madhulika Srikumar and Claire Leibowicz from the Partnership on AI, a nonprofit advancing best practices in AI governance.
AI agents are taking unauthorized actions, from hacking websites to accessing private government files. In many cases, they’ve eluded the very researchers and safety teams tasked with monitoring them.
As agents roll out across critical sectors, from finance to government to medicine, we must be able to monitor them in real time to prevent potentially devastating consequences. And while safety depends on monitoring, monitoring requires
observability
.
​​In other words, we need to know what the agent did and why it did it. Because right now, we’re effectively flying blind when deploying these tools.
Here’s what needs to change
.
Our climate models have a big, dangerous blind spot
Climate change itself increasingly fuels climate change. Rising greenhouse gas concentrations are driving up global temperatures, creating dangerous feedback loops that aren’t fully represented in our climate models—or our emissions-reduction goals.
Scientists have long warned that warming would propel further warming. Now, a growing number of observations and studies are indicating how powerful these cascading effects could be. By extension, they’re also showing how much faster the planet may warm this century.
Read more about the dangerous feedback loops accelerating global warming
.
—James Temple
This article
is from The Spark, our weekly climate tech newsletter.
Sign up
to receive it in your inbox every Wednesday.
Are we there yet? Solid-state batteries
Lithium-ion batteries power everything from personal electronics to grid-scale energy storage, but their liquid electrolytes have drawbacks, not least a troubling tendency to catch fire. Enter the solid-state battery, which swaps liquid for a solid ceramic or polymer.
The technology promises faster charging, longer life, greater energy density and improved safety, and a new generation of companies aims to bring it to market. If their bets pan out, the tech could ease the shift away from fossil fuels.

Title: Le Chonk: Built for Coders, Trusted by Defenders.

URL Source: https://mistral.ai/news/mistral-large-4-oss/

Published Time: 2026-10-29T12:00:07.000Z

Summary

**We release the weights of Le Chonk, advancing the frontier of open models in agentic coding and cybersecurity.**

Earlier this month, we released Mistral Large 4 (Le Chonk), our flagship 1-trillion-parameter, natively multimodal model, in public preview. The response to the preview has exceeded our expectations, and we're grateful to our developer community, early-access customers, and partners for their support, collaboration, and feedback.

Since then, we've put that feedback to work while continuing to scale reinforcement learning, driving massive improvements in **_coding_** and defensive **_cybersecurity_**. Gains continue to accelerate, with no signs of saturation.

**Today, we're releasing the weights of this improved Mistral Large 4.** The new model also features substantial gains in reasoning efficiency that give developers greater performance while lowering inference costs.

Mistral Large 4 ranks as the **best open-weight model for coding** and among the world's most capable open models overall. Trained from scratch on European infrastructure with clear lineage from inception to release, it gives organizations a trusted foundation for Sovereign AI

Mistral is defining the sovereign AI category and leading the open frontier. We're committed to building the world's most capable models and releasing them openly, giving developers, enterprises, and institutions the power to own, customize, and control their AI.

## Built for the Builders.

Mistral Large 4 entered public preview with strong results across leading coding benchmarks. Just three weeks of additional reinforcement learning have since propelled it to the forefront of open-weight coding, taking the lead on FrontierCode and Terminal-Bench while matching the best open-weight models on the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index with substantially greater token efficiency.

On Cognition's private FrontierCode 2.0 benchmark, which assesses end-to-end code quality and whether a repository maintainer would merge the agent's change, Mistral Large 4 leads with a score of 19.7%.

### Cognition - FrontierCode 2.0

## Pushing the pareto frontier for agentic coding.

Mistral Large 4 delivers frontier coding performance with significantly fewer tokens, making sophisticated coding agents more economical to run at scale.

On the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index, Mistral Large 4 scores 48%, effectively tied with the leading open-weight model, GLM-5.3, while using 47% fewer tokens per task on average.

articles.content:
Title: bliki: LLM Voice

URL Source: https://martinfowler.com/bliki/LLM-Voice.html

Markdown Content:
Sometimes when I read a post, I get the growing feeling that I'm reading the output of an LLM. I can't necessarily define why, although there are the common tells (it's not the em-dashes, it's the load-bearing tapestries). As I do this my desire to read on atrophies, sometimes to the point of revulsion

There are tools out there that claim to be able to tell the difference between LLM-written prose and the old-fashioned biological product. I'm wary of them, partly due skeptism about their accuracy, but also because it rather misses the point. The reaction to LLM-Voice is a human one, that sense that we are in an [uncanny valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uncanny_valley) of prose. By the time I'd reach for a tool to tell me what I'm reading, it's already too late, even if it confidently tells me there's no LLM present.

I'm also suspicious of my own ability to accurately recognize LLM voice. Language changes over time, so a common sign of age is complaining about the language of the youngs. I'm inclined to bristle at prose that talks about “adopting a new sales _motion_,” or “a _sharp_ round-up of news”. But I've heard these constructs coming out of human mouths, so that's more a generational difference rather than between carbon and silicon. (And as a transplanted Brit, don't get me started on Americanisms, I'm sure I'll get used to them momentarily.)

Right now I urge authors to be extra-wary of LLM-Voice. In particular I strongly recommend that authors should not fall into the trap of getting the LLM to write a draft. Even if it's edited by a human, it's very hard to expel the LLM-Voice - thus causing the uncanny valley reaction. 1 Even accepting suggestions of rephrasing is dangerous. I have heard of people using LLMs to develop outline and structure, that _may_ be ok, but only as far as an outline. 2 Authors should fill the prose themselves.

1:  Very hard, but not impossible. I've come across one case where I do know the first draft was entirely done by LLM, but I detected no LLM Voice when I read the final piece. It did, however, need a professional editor at a major periodical publication to clean it up.

2:  My policy on this site, is that anyone who uses AI to help them write should declare how they used it, usually in the acknowledgments. This is partly for transparency, and partly so that readers can learn useful ways to use AI. In my own case, I don't use AI for generating prose, nor for help in structure. The only way I use it for writing is as a search tool (but I verify any information by going to the source).

[Say Your Writing](https://martinfowler.com/bliki/SayYourWriting.html) is even more important in the age of LLMs. I habitually speak the words in my head and then write them down (and then edit what I've just written). This advice is particularly important to anyone who has any desire to communicate regularly with writing. Like many things, learning to be a good writer relies on lots of practice. It's a skill worth the time to acquire, but surrendering to an LLM will undermine any progress.

In time it may be that LLMs will be so good that we can't tell the difference. In many ways, that's more worrying. Like most writers, I find writing an almost-essential tool for thinking. Often it's only by writing something down, that I can really get my thoughts on a topic into coherence. I've often started an essay knowing I don't really understand something, but the act of wrestling with the words forces me to overcome my confusions. As more people delegate writing to LLMs they will also delegate thinking and comprehension to LLMs. I don't want to do that, where's the fun of writing then?

Although avoiding LLM-Voice is a general rule, it isn't an absolute one. An important example is that of Jim Highsmith (who contributes to this site). He finds working with an LLM is essential to his writing to [overcome the bane of Parkinson's disease](https://bjsm.bmj.com/content/60/9/677). I'll gladly deal with LLM-Voice in order to continue imbibing my old friend's wisdom.

A more awkward case is that of translation. Many of my colleagues aren't comfortable in English, it is their second or fourth language. Some have found LLM translation an important part to their communication with those of us who know rather less Marathi. But I also would prefer rather a genuine human's clunky prose to the smooth but soulless LLM.

There are situations where it would be reasonable for even a native Englishman to let LLMs write the prose. Such as if I'm writing a form letter to an official, or preparing a report I suspect no-one will ever read 3. Maybe most documentation in the future will only be read by LLMs, and they won't have my uncanny valley worries. But if I want to communicate with humans, my humanity has to shine (or at least ooze) out of my prose.

3:  Michael Nygard commented: “There you really aren't trying to communicate thoughts from one person to other people. You're communicating with a process rather than a human. A human may open the envelope but that person is acting as a component in a cybernetic organism.”

## Notes

1:  Very hard, but not impossible. I've come across one case where I do know the first draft was entirely done by LLM, but I detected no LLM Voice when I read the final piece. It did, however, need a professional editor at a major periodical publication to clean it up.

2:  My policy on this site, is that anyone who uses AI to help them write should declare how they used it, usually in the acknowledgments. This is partly for transparency, and partly so that readers can learn useful ways to use AI. In my own case, I don't use AI for generating prose, nor for help in structure. The only way I use it for writing is as a search tool (but I verify any information by going to the source).

3:  Michael Nygard commented: “There you really aren't trying to communicate thoughts from one person to other people. You're communicating with a process rather than a human. A human may open the envelope but that person is acting as a component in a cybernetic organism.”

## Acknowledgements

I did not use AI or LLMs in any way while writing this post.

articles.content:
Title: Chained PHP2Shell Exploit Roots 25 Servers, including US Government Servers

URL Source: https://dreamgroup.com/blog/chained-php2shell-exploit-roots-25-servers

Published Time: 2026-10-29T18:02:00.659Z

Markdown Content:
_Updated: October 29, 2026._

_Since this discovery, the Dream research team has been sharing updates and collaborating on an investigation with Palo Alto Networks, the vendor of the firewall in question. More information is available [on the Palo Alto Networks website](https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/cve-2026-109618-cve-2026-109619/). Additional details are now included in the post itself._

_Custom PHP2Shell Exploit Chained with Kernel LPE to Root Versions of Palo Alto Networks PAN-OS Firewalls in the Wild_

On October 25, Dream researchers uncovered artifacts of what appeared to be a Chinese AI-assisted campaign that rooted 25 servers, including systems in a US government-affiliated environment. The attacker combined PHP2Shell with a kernel privilege-escalation exploit to compromise exposed systems.

The affected devices run specific versions of Palo Alto Networks PAN-OS.

The exploited surface is the PAN-OS management web server, which also fronts the GlobalProtect portal. Palo Alto Networks’ Unit 42 has independently verified the attacker’s tooling and results, and Palo Alto Networks is releasing fixed PAN-OS versions across the affected branches.

After rooting the firewalls, the attacker launched attacks against Active Directory. The recovered artifacts confirm credential extraction and directory enumeration.

The operation illustrates how an exposed management interface can become a path into an organization’s identity infrastructure. For government defenders, vulnerability discovery is just the beginning, after which the real challenge extends from identifying vulnerable systems to understanding and containing the access a compromise makes possible.

_The research below was conducted with proactive threat hunting using Dream’s autonomous cyber research product, [Hero](https://dreamgroup.com/blog/hercules-on-premises-ai-vulnerability-model-ranked-1-on-cybergym)._

## Discovery

Dream researchers identified a complete attack operation that included a custom weaponization of the PHP2Shell exploit chain (CVE-2026-109618/CVE-2026-109619) paired with the Fragnesia kernel privilege escalation (CVE-2026-46300), target lists, exploitation logs, and approximately 40 custom post-exploitation scripts.

This included artifacts of a campaign that had rooted 25 PAN-OS firewall and management servers across the United States, Japan, Taiwan, and South Korea. Once rooted, the attacker zeroed in on three specific servers in a US government-affiliated environment.

The discovered artifacts revealed an operation that began with exploit development in a lab environment and ended with persistent access to a US government organization's internal Active Directory domain.

### AI Usage in Attack

We also observed some evidence of AI-assisted tooling in the attack infrastructure:

*   Claude Code had been installed
*   An AI-powered offensive security platform called aiscan was configured with Chinese LLMs DeepSeek and Kimi
*   API keys for the Chinese reconnaissance platform FOFA were present

While we have no direct evidence that the AI tools were specifically used to write the exploit or the post-exploitation scripts, the code structure, commenting style, and consistency across ~40 scripts suggest AI-assisted development. That said, this operation does not appear to be a [fully autonomous nation-state attack](https://dreamgroup.com/blog/inside-a-multi-agent-ai-framework-used-to-compromise-government-entities-in-asia).

## The Exploit: Two Vulnerabilities Chained Into One Request

The attacker developed two separate exploits and chained them together to achieve root access on any internet-facing PAN-OS firewall running a vulnerable build in a single HTTP request without any credentials.

### PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618 / CVE-2026-109619) — Remote Code Execution

The implementation we recovered is a custom, non-public build, not a copy of any known public exploit for PHP2Shell. It follows the same underlying concept but appears to have been independently developed and tailored specifically for PAN-OS.

The vulnerability targets PHP's `session.upload_progress` mechanism on the PAN-OS management web server (appweb). PAN-OS uses PHP 8.0.30 with a high memory limit that enables the memory corruption stages of the attack.

The attack works in four orchestrated stages:

*   **A1 — Memory Exhaustion (~383MB):** The attacker floods the server with crafted multipart POST requests, each containing massive filenames and session progress data. This pushes PHP's memory allocator to its limits, forcing the system into a predictable memory layout.
*   **B1 — Information Leak:** A second request forges the stale session ID length from A1, forcing an out-of-bounds read. The server's `Set-Cookie` response header carries the leaked pointer value — giving the attacker the base address of `libphp.so` in the running process.
*   **A2 — Stale Reference Setup (~500MB):** Another round of memory pressure initializes a session, leaving `http_session_vars` as a live `zend_reference`, then triggers a second OOM that leaves `mod_data=NULL` — creating a stale reference the attacker can forge in B2.
*   **B2 — Code Execution:** The final request forges a PHP HashTable entry in the freed memory region. The forged entry's `pDestructor` callback points to `zif_system` (PHP's `system()` function), and its data points to a shell command string. When PHP's cleanup handler walks the HashTable, it calls the forged destructor — executing arbitrary commands as the `nobody` user.

### Fragnesia (CVE-2026-46300) — Kernel Privilege Escalation

Getting code execution as `nobody` isn't enough since SELinux confines `httpd_t` from modifying system files. In order to complete the root, the attacker chained in a second exploit: a Linux kernel vulnerability in the XFRM ESP-in-TCP subsystem.

Fragnesia uses page-cache writes to overwrite `/etc/pam.d/su` — replacing its authentication rules with `pam_permit.so` (accept all). Because the PAM file is only 774 bytes, the exploit uses a per-byte splicing variant to write it precisely. After the overwrite, `su root` succeeds without a password.

Both exploits run in a single B2 HTTP request. The total chain — from unauthenticated HTTPS connection to persistent root webshell — completes in under 15 minutes.

## The Lab: Version Profiling at Scale

The exploit is not a single fire-and-forget payload. It requires precise memory offsets that differ between PAN-OS versions — the address of `zval_ptr_dtor`, the address of `zif_system`, HashTable structure sizes, and memory geometry parameters that control the heap layout during each stage.

Among the recovered artifacts, we found 11 JSON version profile files — one for each PAN-OS version that had been tested:

| PAN-OS branch | PHP | Profiles | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 11.1 | 7.4.33 | 2 provisional | PHP 7.4 — RCE as nobody verified in lab, but full chain not calibrated (base build plus one hotfix variant) |
| 12.1, 12.2 | 8.0.30 | 1 calibrated, 8 provisional | One base profile fully lab-tested; the others inherit its geometry or share offsets with neighboring builds |

Each profile contains the exact offsets extracted from the `libphp.so` binary of that version — with SHA256 hashes of each library, ELF build IDs, and precise memory geometry parameters (chunk sizes, fill counts, drain counts, spray offsets) tuned through lab testing.

The difference between "calibrated" and "provisional" profiles is notable — calibrated means the attacker tested the exploit against a running VM of that version and confirmed the memory geometry works. Provisional means they calculated offsets from the binary but haven't verified on a live instance.

## The Campaign Funnel: From 19,000 Discovered to 25 Exploited

**_Figure 1: Operational timeline of the campaign, from setup on October 8 through exploitation, the pivot into the internal network, and post-exploitation on October 24._**

With the exploit ready and profiles for 9 exploitable versions, the attacker launched a targeting campaign that followed a clear funnel:

### Stage 1: Global Discovery (19,000 targets)

Using FOFA — a Chinese internet asset search engine similar to Shodan — the attacker identified approximately 19,000 internet-facing PAN-OS firewalls worldwide. These were devices with management interfaces exposed to the internet, discoverable through certificate fingerprints and HTTP response signatures.

### Stage 2: Version Fingerprinting (5,000 alive)

A custom version scanner ran with 200 concurrent threads against all 19,000 targets, identifying which devices were actually online and what PAN-OS version they were running. Approximately 5,000 responded with version information.

### Stage 3: Geographic and Version Filtering (240 targets)

From the 5,000 alive devices, the attacker filtered to servers located in only United States, Japan, Taiwan, and South Korea. They then further filtered to versions matching their exploit profiles (the PAN-OS 12.1 and 12.2 branches running PHP 8.0.30). This produced a final target list of 240 firewalls.

Since US, Japan, Taiwan, and South Korea are the four primary strategic adversaries and intelligence targets for Chinese state-aligned cyber operations in the Pacific theater, this indicates potential nation-state adversary efforts.

### Stage 4: Automated Exploitation (24 rooted)

The 240 targets were fed into an automated batch runner that exploited them five at a time, with an 1800-second (30-minute) timeout per target. For each success, the batch:

*   Ran the full PHP2Shell + Fragnesia chain
*   Planted a 103-byte PHP root webshell in a publicly accessible directory on the firewall (`/unauth/php/change_password.php`)
*   Verified root by executing `id` through the webshell
*   Logged the target's hostname and IP to a success CSV
*   Moved to the next target

At this point, 24 firewalls had been successfully rooted.

### Stage 5: Triage (2 firewalls prioritized)

For 22 of the 24 rooted firewalls, the attacker did nothing beyond planting the webshell. No persistence, no tunnels, no post-exploitation tools. The servers were effectively **owned and parked**, allowing the attacker to return through the webshell at any time.

Two servers seemingly associated with one target progressed beyond this stage. Both appeared to belong to a US government-affiliated environment.

### Stage 6: The Pivot (Shifting from Firewall to Domain)

Among the 24 rooted firewalls, two belonged to a US government-affiliated organization. The running configuration extracted from the first firewall revealed an environment with characteristics suggesting government affiliation: CAC (Common Access Card) authentication, a specific naming prefix, and standardized government-style asset naming. The configuration file contained the organization's complete internal network topology: domain controllers, a central firewall management server, a Keycloak SSO server, a GitLab instance, GlobalProtect VPN gateways, and the Active Directory domain.

The first firewall was rooted on Oct 23 at 18:14 UTC during the automated batch. But it crashed shortly after — likely from the ~900MB of exploit traffic — and never came back online. The attacker monitored it with 240 automated probes over two hours, waiting for it to recover. It didn't. The second firewall, whose certificate data definitively linked it to the target organization, had timed out during the original batch.

Recognizing the organization's value from the first firewall's configuration, the attacker created a separate, dedicated campaign and successfully exploited it on Oct 24 at 10:09 UTC.

Within hours, the attacker:

**Built a persistent tunnel into the internal network.**

Title: Agents in Games

URL Source: https://labs.ycombinator.com/projects/games/index.html

Published Time: Thu, 29 Oct 2026 06:27:13 GMT

Markdown Content:
October 2026

**Note:** We're running a new Minecraft colony with 25 GPT-6.1 Terra agents. [Follow on Twitch](https://www.twitch.tv/yc_labs_josh)

Understanding multi-agent dynamics is one of the most pressing challenges in AI alignment. Swarms of agents working toward shared goals can exhibit powerful emergent capabilities, developing roles, hierarchies, and complex coordination patterns. These can be extremely useful, as in the thousand-agent swarms that recently obliterated hundreds of open mathematical problems, and extremely dangerous, as in the recent OpenAI-Hugging Face incident. Like biology, studying agent dynamics requires both formal models (to describe the range of possible behaviors) and empirical research (to see what behaviors arise in practice).

We teamed up with [Olam Labs](https://olamlabs.ai/), which builds multi-agent environments for frontier labs, to run a series of experiments in Minecraft and Mindustry.

## Minecraft

Minecraft is a natural environment for studying swarm behavior. Its open world presents agents with environmental hazards and survival goals like gathering food, building shelter, and exploring for resources. It's also familiar, fun, and has a history as an AI testing ground, from OpenAI's [video pretraining work](https://openai.com/index/vpt/) to Google DeepMind's agents [defeating the Ender Dragon](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22319).

We wanted long-running agents that could play Minecraft. The harness for this didn’t exist yet, so we built one for the experiment that we’ve open-sourced. Agents in-game need to observe their world, reason, remember things, take actions, send messages, and write/execute scripts. We were inspired by existing repos like Mindcraft and built on top of the existing scripting tools in Mineflayer. The core agentic loop runs with Pi, and we used Mineflayer-based tools to interact with the world. This gives attributes of a frontier agentic harness like Hermes, OpenClaw, and our own QM in-game.

[github.com/yc-software/minecraft-agent-harness](https://github.com/yc-software/minecraft-agent-harness)

### Civ50

50 GPT-6.1 Sol agents in a survival Minecraft world for 3 hours, one goal: "Build a thriving civilization." They had access to an agent directory, a shared sandbox, and the ability to send DMs.

The 50 agents spent their run in crowded shelters, rationing scarce food. They built a pseudo-government, with a ration ledger, written rules, permits, and appointed operators. They sent about 5,900 messages.

At first things were very active. Agents spread out and started exploring their map. They were specifically fixated on harvesting trees. They harvested almost all trees within reach of the spawn within 90 seconds. A hierarchy was formed based on the directory order. Ada, who was first, became the de facto leader. Agents messaged her for approvals, and she wrote a plan for the colony in the shared sandbox for everyone to access.

`plans/settlement.md`[Download](https://labs.ycombinator.com/civ50/shared-machine/plans/settlement.md)
```
Settlement coordination (Ada)
Primary storage Greta: (1526,70,1507), crafting table (1526,70,1505).
Other storage Mabel: double chest (1510,71,1516); Cleo: (1526,71,1523).
Cleo building hub shelter; Bram stone mining.
Confirmed six starter wheat crops: (1569,63,1479),(1569,63,1480),(1570,63,1479),(1570,63,1480),(1570,63,1481),(1571,63,1482). Preserve farmland, expand riverside farming. Do not harvest immature wheat.
