articles.title: What we know so far about Spain train crash
articles.content:
Title: Spain train crash: What we know after two trains crashed with dozens feared dead

URL Source: https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cm8xz7pkd0jjo

Published Time: 2026-10-28T11:16:19.600Z

Markdown Content:
## What we know so far about deadly Spain train crash

4 hours ago

Vicky Wong

Two trains crashed south of the Spanish capital Madrid on Wednesday morning, on the high-speed line to Seville.

At least 69 people were killed and dozens injured in the collision, when a state-operated Renfe high-speed train smashed into the back of a stationary train operated by the Iryo company near the town of Urda.

It is one of the worst rail disasters in Europe's modern history, and Spain's worst crash since 2013. Three days of national mourning have been declared in the country.

Here is what we know about the crash so far.

## Where and when did the crash happen?

The crash happened at 08:53 (07:53 GMT) between municipalities Mora and Orgaz, and about 140km (100 miles) south of Madrid, according to an account given by the Spanish government.

The privately run Iryo train **was** stationary on the state-run Renfe train barrelled into the back of it at high speed. Iryo said its train was "struck from behind" by a Renfe train "due to causes that are still unknown".

The crash caused some carriages to fall down an embankment.

All train traffic on the line was stopped at stations along the route.

Renfe said services between Madrid, Ciudad Real and Andalusia were suspended.

A passenger on board one of the trains told local media there was a heavy impact about 40 minutes into the journey.

## What caused the crash?

Spanish Transport Minister Óscar Puente said a computer failure at about 08:30 on Wednesday morning led to the initial halt of six moving trains, including the two trains that subsequently collided.

"In the event of a system failure, the control centre takes over," he said, adding it was the control centre that decided to allow the trains to move again, without any speed restrictions.

That decision, Puente said, was made "under inexplicable circumstances". It resulted in the Renfe train crashing into the Iryo train, which was stationary on the tracks about 25km (15 miles) ahead.

1vanta3 / X via Anadolu / Getty Images

Audio recordings obtained by Spanish media between train controllers working in Madrid for a rail infrastructure company in Adif in Madrid and the train drivers appear to show that one high-speed train was given clearance to move at 08:36 even though another one ahead had stalled.

In one recording, the controller tells the driver of the Renfe train to disconnect and reconnect the LZB mechanism that monitors train speeds, and then resume the journey at normal speed.

"Disconnect and reconnect LZB. Continue your journey and then proceed under [Lateral Signalling Block], at normal speed with normal operation," the control centre operator says to the driver.

The driver replies, "At normal speed?" To which the controller says: "Yes."

Under normal protocols, the driver would be expected to continue moving at a maximum of 40km/h according to their line of sight, and not at normal speed on a track designed for speeds of up to 200km/h.

The Lateral Signaling Block is a back-up or alternative train system used when the automatic signalling or data transmission system fails.

In a second audio recording between the driver of the Iryo train in front and the control centre, the driver says the train "is stationary in front of the entry signal at Urda". After some exchanges, the control centre operator tells the driver to "resume the journey" normally.

The Iryo driver then contacts the control centre again, according to a later recording, saying they cannot start the train. "The train won't allow me to control the [security] system. That's why I am still stopped in front of the entry signal," they say.

The latter recording suggests that the controller had been notified that the Iryo train remained stationary as the Renfe train approached.

## How many passengers were on board?

EPA

Aerial footage shows the extent of the damage and the emergency response

More than 540 people were on board both trains.

Esther Padilla, spokesperson for the government of Castilla-La Mancha region, told TVE that one of the trains - managed by the Iryo company - was carrying 146 passengers plus one baby, while the Renfe-managed train had 397 passengers on board.

Julieta Gallego, a 24-year-old Spanish female long jumper, and former government minister Fátima Báñez, 59, [were among those killed](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cr78plp1p9yvo) in the crash.

More than 100 people were treated for injuries, according to Spanish authorities, and by the next day 50 of them were still in hospital, 15 in a critical condition.

## How have the authorities responded?

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has said "the whole of Spain is grieving" and that "lives have been shattered, families have been torn apart".

"The pain is immense," he said on a visit to the crash site.

The government was "trying to determine what was the origin of this tragedy, of this terrible accident," he added.

"We will get to the bottom of this, and if there has been any negligence, it will come to light.

"If there have been failures in the security system, they will be addressed with the utmost firmness."

Opposition conservative leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo, whose People's Party leads most opinion polls ahead of 29 November elections, said it was not the day to talk about political responsibility, but insisted "Spain has the right to know what is going on with its infrastructure".

Most Spanish politicians cancelled all public engagements on Wednesday and suspended their election campaign.

However, Santiago Abascal of the far-right Vox refused to take part in what his party described as attempts to "use mourning to silence criticism" of the country's rail infrastructure.

Europa Press via Getty Images

A huge emergency response is under way

Three days of official mourning began on Thursday.

Spain's royal family posted on X that it was "shocked and concerned" and expressed condolences for the relatives of the deceased and those affected by the crash.

A spokesperson for the EU said the bloc was ready to help Spain if needed.

A huge emergency response was under way with fire crews and helicopters at the scene.

Hospitals in the area suspended planned surgeries as they deal with an influx of patients from the crash, Spanish media have reported.

A blood transfusion centre in Madrid appealed for "urgent" donations. In a post on X, Centro de Transfusión said it made the request "in the face of a possible sudden increase in care needs".

It reported that facilities in Toledo, Ciudad Real and Alcázar de San Juan had cancelled procedures as casualties from the crash begin to arrive.

The Spanish Civil Guard set up bureaus in Madrid, Toledo, Seville and Córdoba to investigate reports of missing persons.

"The top priority is the identification of the missing persons and the taking of DNA samples to be able to locate their relatives," the civil guard wrote in a post on X.

This is the second high-speed rail tragedy in Spain this year.

In January [a high-speed train derailed in southern Spain](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/clye22ljxw4o), its rear carriages going into the path of a state-run Renfe train, claiming the lives of 46 people.

Title: Zombie Stats: Where the Numbers AI Quotes Come From Research

URL Source: https://trakkr.ai/trakkr-research/zombie-stats

Published Time: 2026-10-28T08:00:00Z

Markdown Content:
## Following one number back to its source

We asked ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini, Claude and Google’s AI Overviews 200 questions that call for a number, the kind people ask every day. Then we clicked the citations, and kept clicking. Here is one trail, from the answer to the end.

Google AI Overviews

What percentage of salespeople give up after one follow-up?

44% of salespeople give up after just one follow-up attempt.

*   44%
*   44%
*   44%
*   44%
*   44%

A sales firm’s stats page 2020
44% of salespeople give up after one follow-up attempt (source).

A freelance writer’s sample article by 2017
80 Percent of Sales Require 5 Follow-up Calls after Meeting; 44 Percent Salespeople Give Up After One Follow-up

**No study behind it**This page cites no research.

1.   In the answer
Every assistant got the same question: “What percentage of salespeople give up after one follow-up?” All five assistants gave the same figure, and only ChatGPT said the evidence behind it was unclear.

2.   One click in
Google AI Overviews cited a sales firm’s stats page, from 2020. The number is right there. Its “source” link goes to a writing sample.

3.   Two clicks in
That leads to a freelance writer’s sample article, online by 2017. The number is in its headline. It lists two slide decks, a blog list and two news stories. None is a study of follow-ups.

4.   The end of the trail
That’s where the trail ends. We tried every other route to this number we could find, and each one stopped at a page that cites no research. This is what we mean by a zombie stat: a number that keeps getting repeated with no study behind it.

Most numbers aren’t like this one. The trouble is that you can’t tell which ones are from the answer. This one came with the same confident tone and the same kind of citation as any other, and all five assistants agreed on it. So we followed 1,285 statistics the same way.

## Fewer than half lead back to a study

We took a random sample of the statistics each assistant cited, 1,285 in all, and walked every trail the same way: the cited page, then that page’s source, up to five pages deep. Where a page named a source without a link, we searched for it.

40% reached a study that says the same thing. Another 8% reached the study, but the number or its context had changed on the way. The rest never got there: 40% stopped at a source we couldn’t check, because it was locked, gone or silent on the number, and 11% led nowhere at all.

### Four in ten trails reached a study that says the same thing

Each square is one in a hundred of the 1,285 statistics we traced, sorted by where its trail ended.

*   40%Sourced We found the study, and it says the same thing.
*   8%Changed We found the study, but the number, who was asked, where or when is different.
*   40%Can’t check A page names a real source, but the number isn’t in it, or the source is locked or gone.
*   11%Nowhere No study anywhere on the trail. Every page repeats the number and credits no one.

The last 1%: trails whose pages wouldn’t load for us.

Trakkr Research, five AI assistants asked 200 questions that call for a number, October 2026. A random sample of each assistant’s cited statistics, weighted by how many each quoted, and corrected with 150 trails checked by hand. Sourced: 40%, 95% range 34% to 46%.

ChatGPT did best, and quoted the fewest numbers: 1.3 per answer, against 6.8 for Claude. The other four landed between 38% and 46%, too close to rank.

### ChatGPT quoted the fewest numbers, and sourced the most

The same hundred squares for each assistant, from its own sample of cited statistics.

**57%** sourced

1.3 statistics per answer

To check this wasn’t down to the questions we picked, we also traced 300 statistics from Google AI Overviews answers to real everyday searches. 40% were sourced, about the same share.

## AI mostly cites pages that repeat the number

The AI mostly wasn’t making numbers up. The page it cited had the figure 82% of the time. But only 21% of the pages cited for a number were the original research.

More than half were company blogs. Add news stories and statistics roundups and you have most of the citations: pages that repeat figures from somewhere else, often without linking to it.

### How often each kind of cited page led to the study

Every page an assistant cited first for a number, by kind. Each column’s width is its share of those citations. Green is how often its trails reached a study that says the same thing.

The first page made a big difference. When a trail started at a research firm or a government page, it reached a matching study 61% of the time. From a company blog, 37%; from a statistics roundup, 35%. Even research firms fell short 38% of the time, often because the full report sat behind a form.

A citation tells you where the AI found a number, not where the number came from.

## Some numbers change along the way

Reaching the study didn’t always mean the number held. Of the statistics that got there, 17% had changed on the way. The digits moved only about one time in four. Usually it was the context: what was measured, the year, the source, or who was asked.

A 2004 study watched 15 British women judge health websites, and 94% of their comments about rejecting a site were about design. Twenty years of retelling made it “94% of first impressions are design-related”, and Google AI Overviews states it as fact.

Ask five assistants the same question and you’ll often get five different numbers. On 28 of the 71 questions where all five gave a percentage, we got four or five different figures.

*   **Perplexity****Approximately 81%** of marketing organizations use marketing automation.

*   **Gemini**Across major industry benchmarks, **between 70% and 79%** of marketers and companies use marketing automation tools in some capacity

*   **Claude****96%** of marketers have used a marketing automation platform or plan to use one

*   **AI Overviews**Roughly **49% to 51%** of companies and marketing teams currently use marketing automation tools, according to industry benchmarks from Moosend and related research studies.

Title: GitHub - SheepSeb/tinyworldformer: Tiny world model generates games and stream ac plays them all on Pico 2W

URL Source: https://github.com/SheepSeb/tinyworldformer

Markdown Content:
Using 2 small neural networks to generate and play the game at the same time on a Raspberry Pi Pico 2 W. The first one creates the game: given the current frame and the action, it predicts the next frame and the reward. The second one plays that game: it uses the generated frame and picks an action.

|  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  |  |  |  |

Every frame above was sampled by the world model network, and the actions were taken by the actor network.

## Why

I got interested in looped transformers, where one transformer block is applied several times with the same weights instead of stacking different layers. Reusing weights is cheap on memory, so I wanted to see if a looped world model could be small enough to run on a microcontroller. I picked the Pico 2 W because it is cheap and has an FPU, and small games because I could write the real versions directly into numpy and check every generated frame against them. Later I added a streaming RL agent so the board could also learn to play inside its own dream.

Contents: [the two networks](https://github.com/SheepSeb/tinyworldformer#the-world-model-and-the-actor) · [the games](https://github.com/SheepSeb/tinyworldformer#the-games) · [the world model](https://github.com/SheepSeb/tinyworldformer#how-the-world-model-works) · [the agents](https://github.com/SheepSeb/tinyworldformer#the-agents-stream-x) · [quantization](https://github.com/SheepSeb/tinyworldformer#quantization-and-the-pico) · [on the chip](https://github.com/SheepSeb/tinyworldformer#on-the-chip) · [flashing](https://github.com/SheepSeb/tinyworldformer#flashing-a-game-and-an-agent) · [browser](https://github.com/SheepSeb/tinyworldformer#in-the-browser) · [reproduce](https://github.com/SheepSeb/tinyworldformer#reproduce) · [code layout](https://github.com/SheepSeb/tinyworldformer#code-layout)

## The world model and the actor

|  | network 1: the world model | network 2: the actor |
| --- | --- | --- |
| job | frame + action → next frame + reward | frame → action |
| architecture | looped transformer, q int8 | MLP with two hidden layers, float32 |
| size | 26k–131k parameters | 9k–16k parameters |
| cost per frame | 2–8M multiply-adds | 9k–16k multiply-adds |
| trained | on recorded real games ([how](https://github.com/SheepSeb/tinyworldformer#how-the-world-model-works)) | with stream-x, in the real game or inside the dream ([how](https://github.com/SheepSeb/tinyworldformer#the-agents-stream-x)) |

The size depends on the game, some games require more parameters to learn them to be playable, we tried to get to keep the number of the parameters small enough.

On the chip neither network ever uses the real game: the actor only sees frames the world model, and the world model only gets actions from the actor. Both run on core 1 of the RP2350, while core 0 handles USB and the display.

The pretrained actor can be swapped for a fresh stream-x agent that learns from scratch on the board. And any button press hands control to you, so you can play the dream yourself.

## The games

Each game is a few hundred lines of numpy in `src/tinyworldformer/games/`. It renders to a small grid of token ids, and one frame always holds the whole game state, so hidden state has to be drawn into the frame: the ball's heading is part of its token, and Doom-lite has a minimap.

| game | frame | rules | random event | world model | exact frames, 2 loops |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Breakout | 20×16 | paddle, ball, 56 bricks, 5 lives | the serve after a miss | 26k params, 4.3M MACs | 99.99% |
| Doom-lite | 32×32 | raycast first-person view of an 8×8 maze; an enemy walks shortest paths to you; you shoot | the enemy's respawn | 55k params, 4.2M MACs | 83.6% (see below) |
| Flappy Bird | 24×24 | gravity, flaps, scrolling pipes | the next gap height | 46k params, 2.0M MACs | 100% |
| Pong | 20×32 | you against a CPU paddle that reacts late, first to 5 | the serve after a point | 46k params, 2.3M MACs | 99.45% |
| Pac-Man lite | 48×48 | 23×21 maze, 249 pellets, two ghosts on shortest paths, 3 lives | the ghosts' respawn | 131k params, 8.2M MACs | 86.4% |

"Exact frames" is the share of held-out transitions where every cell of the predicted frame matches the real game. Frames right after a random event are left out, since those can only be sampled, not predicted. Doom-lite's 3D view has 768 cells and a single shaded wall pixel off counts the whole frame as wrong, so its number looks worse than it plays; the game state is almost always right (see [checking the dream](https://github.com/SheepSeb/tinyworldformer#checking-the-dream)).

You can play the real games in a terminal: `uv run python -m tinyworldformer.games.play --game pacman` (or `breakout`, `doomlite`, `flappy`, `pong`).

## How the world model works

### Frames split into tokens

The frame is cut into square patches: 2×2 cells in Breakout, 4×4 in Doom-lite, Flappy Bird and Pong, 6×6 in Pac-Man. That gives 36 to 80 tokens per game. A patch's embedding is the sum of one learned vector per cell, with a separate table for each position inside the patch so the cell order isn't lost. Every token also gets a position vector and the action's vector.

### Looped Transformer

The model is a single transformer block (attention plus a ReLU MLP) with one set of weights, applied 1 to 4 times, with the input added back before every pass. The output after every pass is trained against the next frame, so at run time the loop count trades speed for accuracy. On the Pico to keep a decent frame rate we use uses two loops.

The animation shows one held-out Doom-lite step. After one pass the model draws an enemy that isn't there, and each further pass removes part of it: 92, 35, 12, then 0 wrong cells. The bars on the right are the share of held-out frames each loop count gets exactly right.

Here is a dreamed Doom-lite step decoded after 1, 2, 3 and 4 loops, with red boxes on cells that differ from the real rules:

Exact held-out frames by loop count:

| loops | Breakout | Doom-lite | Flappy Bird | Pong | Pac-Man |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 99.68% | 59.8% | 99.99% | 98.47% | 79.6% |
| 2 | 99.99% | 83.6% | 100% | 99.45% | 86.4% |
| 3 | 100% | 85.9% | 100% | 99.60% | 85.7% |
| 4 | 99.96% | 84.7% | 100% | 99.53% | 84.4% |

### Decoding

The model outputs a score for every cell and every token. Turning those scores into a frame turned out to matter almost as much as the model, and it ended up as three rules (shown above on Pong):

1.   Background cells (walls, bricks, pellets, floor) each take their most likely token independently.
2.   Singletons (the ball, the player, each ghost) are placed with one choice over all (cell, token) pairs, so there is always exactly one of each. After a random event the choice is sampled among candidates within 2.2 logits of the best, so the world model samples a new serve or respawn instead of averaging them.
3.   Pac-Man and the ghosts are 2×2 sprites, but only one cell of each carries state (the mouth holds the heading; the ghost's lower-left cell holds whether a pellet is underneath). The other three cells are stamped from it instead of predicted.

We implemented Rule 2 because the first Breakout model drew two balls at once; one global choice took exact frames from 91.6% to 99.7%.

### Checking the world model

Accuracy on recorded data wasn't enough. An agent drives the dream into states the data never had, and any mistake there is something it can exploit. So the main check runs while an agent plays: read the game state back off the dreamed frame (`games/<game>.py: read`), apply the real rules to that state and the agent's action, and compare the result with the next dreamed frame and reward.

5,000 dreamed steps per game at 2 loops, with the shipped agent (`training/evalwm.py --agent`):

| game | wrong game states | wrong rewards | wrong cells per step |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Breakout | not read back; 0 frames with impossible tokens | 6 (paid without a brick breaking) | – |
| Doom-lite | 1 | 0 | 1.50 |
| Flappy Bird | 0 | 0 | 0.00 |
| Pong | 1 | 0 | 0.00 |
| Pac-Man | 742 | 38 | 0.39 |

### Training

First, agents play the real game and every step is recorded as one example (frame, action, next frame, reward), 1–3 million per game. Some episodes start from unusual states, like bricks with holes or random positions, so the data covers more of the game.

Then the world model learns to predict the next frame with a per-cell cross-entropy loss: 30k steps, with the first 3–4k steps run in float, then int8 rounding switches on ([QAT](https://github.com/SheepSeb/tinyworldformer#quantization-and-the-pico)).

The int8 weights are written into Rust source with every float stored as its exact bits. We check them with `cargo test` to reproduces the Python integer spec bit for bit, and then the firmware runs on the Pico.

An agent trained in the world model reaches states the recorded data never had, so record real games with that agent and fine-tune the world model on everything.

The agent in different games stated exploiting them so those are some fixes to it:

*   Weighting the loss by "this cell changed" biased the model toward predicting change, so it drew two balls and broke two bricks. Weighting by where things can happen in the input frame, plus the global singleton choice, fixed it.
*   A Breakout agent in the dream got 154 points with 26 bricks left, because the world model didn't remove bricks from the corner when it were hit. Doom-lite agents learned to snipe from 5 cells away.
*   Agents trained only in the dream scored 210 there (the real maximum is 56) and 28 in the real game, as _World Models_ (Ha & Schmidhuber) predicts. Each collect-and-fine-tune round closed the exploit that agent had found.
*   The Doom-lite dream sometimes lost the enemy sprite and never drew it again: the model copied the previous view instead of redrawing it from the minimap. Noise augmentation fixed it (`train --noise 0.3`, as in GameNGen): input views get random pixels and sometimes lose the sprite.
*   `d=32` couldn't absorb the wider Breakout data and `d=48` could. Pac-Man's 48×48 frame needed `d=64`.

## The agents: stream-x

The agents use Stream AC(λ) (Elsayed, Vasan & Mahmood, 2024), which learns from one transition at a time: no replay buffer, no batches, no target network. Eligibility traces carry credit back in time, and ObGD shrinks any step that would overshoot the TD target. The policy and value networks each have two hidden layers of 64 units (32 on the Pico) with LayerNorm.

The input is a feature vector read off the frame (`training/streamx.py: observe_*`, mirrored in Rust in `tinyworldformer-rs/src/agent.rs`). For example, the ball's row, column and heading in Breakout, or in Pac-Man, for each direction, the shortest-path distance to the nearest pellet and how close each ghost is.

Each panel plays greedily from the same start and skips a few steps per frame. "try" counts the episodes played so far, so you can see the crashes.

articles.title: Claude Duet is the first personal-assistant-type harness that feels useful
articles.content:
Title: Duet is the future of chatbot interaction — fig.blue

URL Source: https://fig.blue/posts/duet-is-the-future/

Markdown Content:
_Written by a human. Not affiliated with Anthropic._

Look, I really didn’t want to like Duet. I don’t want to be an Anthropic fanboy and it annoys me when they do things better than the competition. But they have done it again.

I have given serious effort to Muse, Dot, NanoClaw, and a host of other personal-assistant-type harnesses. Duet is the first one that felt more useful than tedious, and it feels like a serious evolution of the chat experience rather than another “give me all your credentials to be useful” agent. Here’s why I like it so far.

### 1. It’s fast

Other assistant apps are always doing who-the-hell-knows-what in the background while I wait for a response. Duet clearly prioritizes getting a snappy response to the user even if background work is needed. It’s supposedly powered by Opus 5.5, but I’ve never seen Opus move this fast in other Claude UIs. Clearly some tuning went on here. This is critical to be a useful assistant: If you want to be my shell to the world, I am not going to sit and twiddle my thumbs between commands.

### 2. Channels are neat

Maybe I’m just Slack-brained, but I really like Duet channels. In particular: I like that Duet can create and manage channels for me. One tedious aspect of working with LLMs is trying to keep track of chat sessions: workstreams get lost, context must be carefully maintained, sessions get misnamed, etc.

Duet does the tedious session organizing for me. A natural hierarchy has emerged for my work, and I suspect I will have fewer lost threads with Duet. `Cmd-k` was already reflex for me: it pulls up the list of channels and lets me rapidly swap between them. Channels can also see and reference each other so Duet can help me keep work in the right lane.

### 3. Access policies are meaningful

Access to Github repos is restricted per channel. I can add a few related repos to a specific channel, and not worry that the channel might commingle work from my other projects.

It also never tries to get my credentials. This is my pet peeve with most assistant apps: they won’t do much until you hand them the keys. Muse has a credential store, which at least makes the agent blind to the values, but it could still enter those in something untrusted.

Duet stores no credentials and actively discourages being given them. At best it might let you login via a Chrome session on its behalf. But it has never asked me to do that: it prefers to use the connector ecosystem Claude already has, and seems content to stay in its lane otherwise.

### 4. Responses are short

This isn’t unique to Duet, Dot and Muse seem to get this too: Nobody wants to read a full page response to a simple question, which has been the de facto chatbot experience for years. I have always had to add a bunch of instructions trying to persuade my agents to give succinct responses. They all can also add emoji “reactions” to messages, though I find that personality makes a difference here: Muse tended to thumbs up everything, whereas Duet uses it to give me an okay without elaborating further, and I find that delightful.

### THAT BEING SAID

It’s in beta, and definitely has some glitches. Sometimes threads are running but not visible. I’ve seen delegated repo access fail to attach correctly (race condition between agent start and access attachment?).

I also acknowledge my use-cases likely make Duet a better fit for me in particular. Muse might be a better fit for others. YMMV.

And Dot still reigns on voice interaction. Anthropic doesn’t even seem to care about having a conversational voice mode, it’s still just glorified speech-to-text.

### Duet is already replacing most of my AI workflows

I don’t really enjoy the management side of managing agents: remembering who is running and with what context where. There is always some agent somewhere waiting on me to make a decision or follow up on some task. I’m sure some agent did brilliant work for me on a box somewhere that I’ve neglected and will be forgotten forever.

The innovation that matters to me most is the hierarchy of concerns: The top level of Duet has a bird’s eye view of all my workstreams, but no low-level access. The channels carry more access, but under more constrained context. Sub-threads spun up by the channels can be even further constrained as they work in specific code sandboxes. The Desktop app can reach local hosts where I let it, and that’s usually only for the QA or deployment edge after the coding is done in the cloud.

Most of this is how I already preferred to arrange my agents, and similar flows could be hacked together with some ducttape and API credits. Duet just makes this hierarchy a natural part of the core product, and it works so well that I suspect it’s going to be the default experience for all chatbot UIs in the near future.

[Launch HN: Simantic (YC F26) – Firmware Simulation for AI Agents](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50291116) 50 points by [shong0504](https://news.ycombinator.com/user?id=shong0504)[9 hours ago](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50291116) | [hide](https://news.ycombinator.com/hide?id=50291116&goto=item%3Fid%3D50291116) | [past](https://hn.algolia.com/?query=Launch%20HN%3A%20Simantic%20%28YC%20F26%29%20%E2%80%93%20Firmware%20Simulation%20for%20AI%20Agents&type=story&dateRange=all&sort=byDate&storyText=false&prefix&page=0) | [favorite](https://news.ycombinator.com/fave?id=50291116) | [14 comments](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50291116) Hi HN, we're Ahnaf and Seungmin from Simantic ([https://simantic.com](https://simantic.com/)). We are building the simulation layer that lets engineers and AI agents test and validate firmware without hardware. Before Simantic, we were ex-firmware engineers at companies like Neuralink and Tesla. We’ve worked on some of the coolest projects, like the Cybertruck and Roadster, back when they were still early prototypes. We started working on firmware back when ChatGPT didn’t exist yet, but over the years, we saw how much of the engineering and development work has been automated as the frontier models improved to this point. In software, AI can run and test code inside your computer in a matter of seconds. But as firmware engineers, we didn’t have that luxury. An AI agent can write firmware in seconds, but in order to test it, we had to flash a physical board, then manually run tests using expensive and clunky tools with software made over a decade ago. To speed up the validation loop, we built the simulation layer that lets AI agents test the firmware and make decisions based on evidence, instead of waiting for the engineer to run tests for them. We used to spend hours testing our firmware manually on devboards, but now we use our own simulation to validate firmware in seconds. What we offer: - Virtual devboards you can program and run with a single API call, without leaving your terminal. - An AI code reviewer for firmware, that makes informed decisions based on evidence, using our simulation as a verification engine. - A CI/CD pipeline for your hardware projects that validates your firmware against a simulated version of the microcontroller on every commit. Here is a demo of our simulation used in an AI code review session: [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kBK1ZjGWWbQ](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kBK1ZjGWWbQ) Our users are using Simantic for bare-metal and RTOS development for applications like flight controllers, electric vehicles, robotics, and satellites. For safety critical systems like avionics and automotives, a robust simulation system is incredibly important, because every change in the firmware puts a human life at stake, especially for machines that cost hundreds of thousands to millions of dollars. We recently helped an early stage space startup building satellites, to test their firmware on hardware that they don't yet have. Even the development modules for those satellites costs over $100k, and we helped them do that at just a hundredth of the cost and time. Early on in our journey, we established our idea to make better simulation but didn’t have a clear idea of how we would do it, we considered developing our software around open source emulation frameworks like Renode ([https://github.com/renode/renode](https://github.com/renode/renode)) and QEMU ([https://www.qemu.org/](https://www.qemu.org/)), because they were tools already used within the firmware industry. We built our MVP that was essentially a wrapper around Renode, but we quickly realized there were a lot of limitations to doing this. 1. We were bottlenecked by the development speed of Renode themselves. We tried making contributions on Github to fix issues we came across, but the speed in which we could merge our features in was not fast enough for a startup like us trying to move fast. 2. Renode is built using Dotnet, and it was proving itself to be slower than we would have liked. Renode was released in 2017, which was when all code was still being written by hand, so I think it made sense looking back, but there were limitations because of the language itself. 3. The open source tools were bloated, with features that we would never use. Yes, there were a breadth of features, but we had a lot of things we had to work around just because we couldn’t remove or change them. Users were complaining about simulation accuracy. Renode is an emulator at the core, but our users, especially those who are building systems where timing accuracy is crucial did not find the accuracy good enough to validate their firmware. Because of these issues, we made our own simulation engine from scratch, fully written in Rust. - Our simulation is focused on accuracy. Open source frameworks often focus on expandability and developer experience, which means there were a lot of tradeoffs made to prioritize a breadth of models rather than going deep into a set of select models. - We have our own hardware validation rigs running 24/7 to ensure our simulation models are as close to real world hardware as possible, and any gaps are detected and fixed as soon as we can. It currently looks like devboards connected to a Saleae Logic MSO and a SWD bus, controlled by a Linux PC, running Claude 24/7 just finding these gaps. Our cloud-hosted simulator is available to use right now! We also provide a native binary with our developer plan licenses that let you run your firmware on your machines locally without any limitations. Check it out at [https://simantic.com/cloud-sim](https://simantic.com/cloud-sim), and you can start using our AI firmware reviewer bot in your own Github repos here: [https://simantic.com/dashboard/simantic-bot](https://simantic.com/dashboard/simantic-bot). We currently have support for some models of the STM32F0, F4, H7 series MCUs, ESP32-S3/C3, and RP2040, but we’re constantly working to release new models every week, and improve our existing ones. Title: A Pig, the State, and War: Porco Rosso (Kurenai no Buta)

URL Source: https://journal.animationstudies.org/article/id/66/

**Introduction**
 Historically, animated cartoons and movies have been used as ‘propaganda’ in war (Roffat 2011). Some animated films, however, contribute to conveying an anti-war pacifist point of view (Takai 2011). As such, the film _Porco Rosso_ (1992) can be categorized as “anti-war propaganda” (Okuda 2003, p. 144). Although Miyazaki has been attracted by seaplanes designed and manufactured during the period between the First World War and the Second World War (Kiridoshi 2008, p. 72), this film conveys the important memory of war, especially the interwar era and the post-Cold War world. Indeed, in an interview just before the release of _Porco Rosso_, Miyazaki stated that the film is relevant to the Gulf War, and referred to the Yugoslav Wars as ethnic and nationalistic conflicts (Miyazaki 1996, p. 519; Miyazaki 2002, p. 95). In this context, the film forwards Miyazaki’s anti-war message. This paper examines _Porco Rosso_(_Kurenai no Buta_), which is based on 15 pages of _Hikotei Jidai (_ _The Golden Age of the Flying Boat)_, a comic created by Hayao Miyazaki and released in the animation journal, _Model Graphics_, No.14-16 in 1990 (Kiridoshi 2008, p. 72). A synopsis of the comic story is literally “typed” at the beginning of _Porco Rosso_, as follows: “This motion picture is set over the Mediterranean Sea in an age when seaplanes ruled the waves. It tells a story of a valiant pig, who fought against flying pirates, for his pride, for his lover, and for his fortune. The name of the hero of our story is Crimson Pig.” Scholarship on this film has focused on issues of “war and peace,” especially in terms of the “non-war” (_hisen_) message (e.g. Okuda 2003). Similarly, Kazami et al (2002), among others, (Kano 2006; Kiridoshi 2008) provide some answers to the central question of the film: Why did Porco turn into a pig? The primary reason is that he was traumatized by the war. Building on Kazami et al’s work, this paper attributes the reason that Porco became a pig to the following three aspects: “man, the state and war” (Waltz, 1959). According Kenneth Waltz, theorist of international politics, the causes of war occur on three levels: individual, domestic, and international. Like Waltz, I argue here that Porco became a pig because he hates the following three factors: man (egoism), the state (nationalism) and war (militarism). Accordingly, my analysis of _Porco Rosso_ is situated in the framework of peace research and international relations, such as non-killing philosophy, soft power/hard power, and conflict prevention/conflict resolution.
**Methodology**
 In the field of animation studies, animation films by Studio Ghibli have been frequently analyzed as a case study. Ghibli animation films are “often considered as artistic productions, both entertaining and meaningful” (Gan 2009, p. 36). There are a large number of publications on the Studio Ghibli’s films, particularly those directed by Hayao Miyazaki. Nobuyuki Tsugata (2004), for instance, examined Miyazaki’s works in comparison with the animated cartoons of Osamu Tezuka, the creator of _Astro Boy_ (1963). Miyazaki’s films also have been discussed compared with Disney animation. For instance, Kaori Yoshida (2011) offered a comparative analysis on Disney’s _Pocahontas_ (1995) and Ghibli’s _Princess Mononoke_ (1997) in terms of national identity. Moreover, some scholars (e.g. Kano 2006; Kiridoshi 2008) provided comprehensive thematic or structural analyses of Miyazaki’s films. However, earlier studies on Miyazaki animation, or Miyazaki-related animation films, do not necessarily focus on the issue of war and peace. Therefore, this paper offers an analysis of Miyazaki-related animation films in terms of war and peace (Table 1).  Although the Miyazaki-related films in Table 1 do not directly deal with war themselves, all of them are related to war and peace to a certain extent. _Hols: Prince of the Sun_ (1968) was released in the middle of the Vietnam War (1965-1975) and some combat scenes of the film represent the war. Miyazaki was involved as an animator in the creation of the film with director Isao Takahata, a friend and colleague. _Nausicaä of the Valley of the Wind_ (1984) is a masterpiece, and the film reflects the international politics during the Cold War. The Giant Warrior (_kyoshinhei_) that caused an apocalyptic war, or the Seven Days of Fire, functions as a symbol of nuclear weaponry. The confrontation between Pejite and Tolmekia, the two powerful countries in the story can similarly be regarded as reflection of the Cold War bipolar structure (Akimoto 2014a). _Laputa: Castle in the Sky_ (1986) was also created during the middle of the Cold War. The number of nuclear warheads in the world reached its peak in the mid-1980s, and the military technology of the legendary castle, Laputa, also symbolizes nuclear weapons. In this film, the word, “peace” is used only one time by Muska, who tries to conquer the world by taking possession of Laputa’s military technology. Obviously, this is a “political satire” by Miyazaki (Akimoto 2014b). _Grave of the Fireflies_ (1988), a fictional film about a Japanese boy and his little sister at the end of the Pacific War (1941-1945), was not directed by Miyazaki but instead by Isao Takahata, another Studio Ghibli director (Akimoto 2014c), but reflects similar anti-war sentiment. In the post-Cold War context, Miyazaki produced _Porco Rosso_ (1992) which depicts the interwar period (1919-1939) of the Adriatic Sea in conjunction with the Yugoslavian War (1991). Miyazaki contributed to the creation of _Whisper of the Heart_ (1994) that has a passing reference to the Second World War (1939-1945). _Princess Mononoke_ (1997) deals with Japanese civil war as well as confrontation between humans and animals. _Howl’s Moving Castle_ (2004) and the latest film, _The Wind Rises_ (2013) are related to the 2003 Iraq War, and the Asia Pacific War (1931-1945) (Akimoto 2014d; Akimoto 2014e). Thus, the films in which Miyazaki or Studio Ghibli is involved can be analyzed from a perspective of peace research (peace studies), an academic field which examines causes of war and conditions for peace. While ethical and legal issues need to be carefully taken into consideration when teaching Japanese animation (McLelland 2013), Studio Ghibli animation films can be useful as educational materials at the university level (Yonemura 2003, p. 10), particularly in the fields of both peace research and peace education. From the perspective of peace research, _Porco Rosso_ makes a particularly rich case study, particularly because Miyazaki won the best feature film award in the 1993 Annecy International Animation Film Festival (Annecy.org 2013). Due to the award, which is one of the most internationally prestigious animation film festivals, the film was internationally acclaimed, and Miyazaki characterized as “Walt Disney Nippon” (Christin 1997, p. 184). Most reviews of and scholarship on _Porco Rosso_ tend toward general analysis, lacking a specific focus on war and peace (e.g. Animage 1992, 2011; Kazami et al. 2002; Okuda 2003; Kano 2006; Kiridoshi 2008). Moreover, Miyazaki himself has made similar comments on his own work (Miyazaki 1996, 1997, 2013). Yet, none of the earlier studies of the film have investigated them from a perspective of peace research. In order to examine _Porco Rosso_, which conveys a similar anti-war message to _The Wind Rises_ (_Kaze Tachinu_) (2013), which narrates Japan’s interwar period and war responsibility (Akimoto 2013a), this paper employs an interdisciplinary approach which combines peace research with animation studies. As an analytical method, this paper combines keyword analysis described above with sequence analysis of character’s lines as well as historical events. The sequence analysis is useful tool to examine timeline sequence (Abbott 1995) and it is applicable to film studies with a particular focus on character’s lines in historical context. Accordingly, the five main characters as well as historical background of this film need to be overviewed in this section. First, the hero of this film is a pig, Porco Rosso who flies in his crimson seaplane, SAVOIA S-21. As a bounty hunter, he cracks down on Aero Viking (Sky Pirates) in the Adriatic Sea after the First World War. He used to be a human (Marco Paggot) and the ace pilot of the Italian Air Force, but he decided to leave the army after the war and cursed himself, turning into a pig. As I outline below, Porco was traumatized by his experiences in the war (Animage 2011, p. 35-37). Second, Madam Gina, a childhood friend of Porco and a madam of Hotel Adriano, is one of the two heroines of this film. In the film, it is said that pilots in the Mediterranean Sea tend to fall in love with her and visit Hotel Adriano for her song. She was married to three pilots who were all members of the Flying Club she organized as a child, but all of them died in the Great War, or in a flight accident. Gina is in secret love with Porco and vice versa (ibid, p. 54-57). Third, Fiyo Piccolo, the other heroine, is a 17-year old female mechanic and the granddaughter of Master Piccolo. She repairs Porco’s seaplane and develops an adolescent infatuation with him (ibid, 43-45). Fourth, Donald Curtis, an American pilot and Porco’s rival, is hired by Aero Viking to fight against Porco. He is a competent pilot and has an ambition to first become a Hollywood movie star, and then US President afterwards. Curtis falls in love with Gina at first sight and falls for Fiyo next (ibid, pp. 48-51). Fifth, the Mamma Aiutos, one of the largest Aero Vikings in the Adriatic Sea, steals and kidnaps for a living after the First World War (ibid, p. 63-65). This study examines the five character’s lines in the following historical context as demonstrated by Table 2 below.  At a macro level, the chronology of the interwar period as the historical background for the film needs to be taken into consideration, as this background is crucial in understanding the content of this film. At a micro level, key scenes and main characters’ lines of the film will be examined. This is also imperative to comprehend the implications of the film for the issue of war and peace. The sequence of the nine most significant scenes in the film are as follows: 1) Porco’s “Non-Killing” Policy: Battle with the Mamma Aiutos 2) Gina’s “Soft Power” and “Peaceful Conflict Prevention” 3) Gina’s Life in War and Peace 4) Porco’s Antipathy towards the State and War 5) Fiyo and Repair of Porco’s Fighter Plane 6) The Pig and the Italian Air Force: “Better a Pig than a Fascist” 7) Fiyo’s “Soft Power” and “Peaceful Conflict Resolution” 8) The War and the Spell: Why Did He Turn Into a Pig? 9) Porco’s “Non-Killing” Philosophy in the Final Battle The main characters’ dialogue in these nine sections accordingly constitute the primary source to be carefully investigated, in combination with my earlier argument, and relevant publications as secondary source in the context of the interwar period. The sequence analysis of the film and characters’ lines will be examined by using keywords in peace research and international politics.
